text: You've now got mixed precision, gradient accumulation, multi-GPU training, and torch.compile all available — but applying any of them without measuring first is guesswork. This lesson shows you how to actually find out where a training step spends its time.

torch.profiler.profile is a context manager you wrap around a few training steps, recording CPU and CUDA activity for every operation that runs inside it. Calling prof.step() at the end of each iteration marks a step boundary, which is what lets more advanced scheduling features work correctly.

Once the block exits, key_averages gives you an aggregated table, one row per operation, sortable by whichever time column matters. CPU time is Python and kernel-launch overhead; CUDA time is what the GPU actually spent executing.

If your top rows by CUDA time are matrix multiplies or convolutions, you're compute-bound, and mixed precision and torch.compile are exactly the right tools. If CPU time dominates instead and GPU rows look small, the bottleneck is somewhere else — very often too few DataLoader workers or slow per-sample preprocessing starving the GPU between steps.

For a deeper look than the table gives you, you can point the profiler at a trace handler and open the result in TensorBoard — a timeline view of which operation ran on which stream, and exactly where any gaps are.
That closes out mixed precision and multi-GPU basics. Chapter 8 turns to debugging and experiment tracking — reading what a training run is actually telling you, before and after you've made it fast.
